description:
PERIAPSIS | MMXXVI

PERIAPSIS is a multidisciplinary team focused on aerospace engineering, software, autonomous systems, and emerging technologies. With experience in national and international competitions, including a quantum computing hackathon final, we are joining NASA Space Apps 2026 to tackle "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map." Our project combines NASA data, terrain analysis, risk-aware navigation, and mission planning to support future Mars exploration.
summary:
Martian Map is a browser-based Marswalk planner for the first crews on Mars. It layers real data from four NASA missions (MRO, Mars Odyssey, Mars 2020 and Curiosity) onto one 4 m grid in 3D. It works at two real sites: Jezero crater and the boxwork ridges of Mount Sharp in Gale crater.

A crew picks a science objective. The planner then chooses the most valuable stops, routes two astronauts around steep slopes and rocks, and checks at every point whether they can still walk home. It counts oxygen (NASA BVAD rates), suit and payload mass (NASA's 45 kg carry limit), daylight, radiation and dust. The result is a GO, CONDITIONAL or NO-GO decision with its reasons.

During the simulated EVA, a dust devil triggers a new safe route on the spot. The plan travels with the crew as a wrist console that works offline and an Apollo-style printed cuff card.

On Mars, one wrong turn costs oxygen, and there is no one to ask for directions. Martian Map refuses impossible plans, labels what is simulated or AI-predicted, and is verified by 175 automated tests on real NASA data.
details:
What it does and how it works

Martian Map plans a two-person Marswalk (EVA) for the first crews on Mars, at two real sites: Jezero crater (Perseverance) and the boxwork ridges of Mount Sharp in Gale crater (Curiosity). It layers eight types of NASA data onto one 4 m grid over 2 × 2 km, shown in 3D on 1 m HiRISE terrain. The data come from four missions: MRO HiRISE and CRISM, Mars Odyssey THEMIS, and Perseverance and Curiosity (ChemCam, RAD, MEDA, REMS). It also uses 3,815 rover photos and NASA DONKI space weather.

The app follows a mission in four workspaces:

• 01 Explore: a data catalog where every layer states its source and type (measured, orbital, derived, modelled, simulated or AI-predicted). Click any point for its elevation, slope, hazard and distance home.

• 02 Analyze: hazards, minerals, geology, AI terrain labels, and which data are missing.

• 03 Plan Mission: pick a science objective. The planner chooses the most valuable stops (Held–Karp) and routes the crew by A* on walking time, treating slopes over 20° and big rocks as walls. It offers SAFE, ECO, FAST and AUTO routes, each with an elevation profile.

• 04 Operations: a GO / CONDITIONAL / NO-GO decision with its reasons, then a simulated EVA with a live HUD.

At every point of the route the planner checks whether the crew can still walk home. It accounts for:

• oxygen, using NASA BVAD rates,

• suit and payload mass against NASA's 45 kg carry limit,

• daylight and radiation (Curiosity RAD, DONKI storms),

• dust exposure of suit parts and tools.

If a dust devil appears ahead, the system draws a 25 m safety zone and plans a new SAFE route from where the crew stands. If no safe route exists, they walk back the way they came. The plan reaches the astronaut as a proposed wrist console that keeps working offline, and as an Apollo-style printed cuff card with "leave by" times for each stop.

Benefits and intended impact

On Mars, help is months away and a wrong turn costs oxygen. Martian Map:

• lets astronauts step out knowing they can get back,

• gives planners a ready-made walking map for any site with HiRISE data, instead of hours of manual work,

• gives scientists AI labels for rover photos.

It also shows why decisions change. With the same stops, switching from NASA's Moon EVA limits to our Mars-conservative limits cuts the safety margin at Jezero from 3 h 14 min to 1 h 21 min.

Tools and technologies

• App: JavaScript, React, Three.js (React Three Fiber) and Vite. It runs in any browser on desktop, tablet or phone, with an adaptive layout. An offline package needs only Python 3.

• Data pipeline: Python with rasterio, NumPy and Pillow, which turns NASA/USGS/PDS products into the site grid.

• AI: our own terrain segmentation model, LR-ASPP MobileNetV3, trained with PyTorch on 16,711 NASA/JPL AI4Mars images and exported to ONNX. On expert-labelled tests it reaches IoU 0.93 for soil, 0.87 for sand and 0.85 for bedrock.

• Quality:

• 175 JavaScript tests, many on real site data, and 23 Python tests;

• Playwright browser tests on desktop, tablet and phone;

• ESLint;

• GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for CI and deployment.

• AI assistance: we used Anthropic Claude as a coding assistant under the team's direction. No AI-generated images are used.

• Hardware: none required.

What makes it creative

• It refuses the impossible. You cannot place a waypoint on a slope over 20°, and an overweight or oxygen-short plan is NO-GO, always with the reason shown.

• The plan adapts in real time. A dust devil triggers a re-route, not just a warning.

• Three outputs always agree. The HUD, the wrist console and the printed card are built from one timeline, after the Apollo 15–17 cuff checklists.

• It never presents a guess as a fact. Every layer and number carries its provenance; missing data gives INSUFFICIENT DATA, never GO.

• Its AI model can keep learning from each new mission's photos.

Factors we considered

Crew safety came first: walk-back margin, the point of no return, a 30-min reserve and daylight. NASA's published EVA limits were written for the Moon. NASA's own test found suited walking at Mars gravity costs 1.65× the oxygen, so we added a Mars-conservative limit set. We designed for communication loss (offline console, paper backup) and for readability on a screen across the room. We were honest about limits: oxygen is a model, not a sensor; the dust devil is simulated; and the AI never changes a route.
